summary: This standards-track memo specifies how to store in the DNS the mapping information (MCGAM) that MIXER-conformant gateways need to map RFC 822 domain names to X.400 O/R names and back.

plainLanguage.summary:
Mail systems built on X.400 and on the Internet used different address formats. A gateway that moves mail between them needs a rule telling it how to rewrite one format into the other, and those rules used to live in tables copied to every gateway.

This RFC puts the rules in the DNS instead. Each rule becomes a PX record: one kind of record holds the rules that turn a domain name into an X.400 address, and another part of the DNS tree, reached through a reserved label under each country code, holds the rules that work the other way. A gateway finds what it needs with a single DNS query.

questions: what is the dns px record
how to map x400 addresses to rfc822
subtitle: How a mail gateway finds the rule that turns an X.400 address into a domain name.

tldr.problem: MIXER gateways need a database that maps X.400 addresses to RFC822 domain names and back. The original design kept that database in static tables that had to be distributed to every gateway and updated everywhere at once.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC stores the mapping rules in the DNS as PX resource records. Rules that translate a domain name into an X.400 address live in the ordinary DNS tree, and rules that translate the other way live in a new branch of the name space placed under each country code, under the reserved label X42D.
tldr.outcome: A gateway resolves the mapping with one DNS query, and each organisation publishes and changes its own rules without coordinating with anyone else. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1664 and has since been updated by RFC 3597.

facts.label: Reserved label for the X.400 name space

today: RFC 2163 is a Proposed Standard from January 1998. It obsoletes RFC 1664 and has since been updated by RFC 3597. The document reports that tests were run successfully under a provisional top-level domain when RFC 1664 was developed, and that more than two years of operational experience with RFC 1664 confirmed the method.

sections.title: Why the Mapping Tables Were a Problem
sections.content:
Connectivity between Internet SMTP mail and other mail services, including Internet X.400 mail and commercial X.400 service providers, is assured by the Mail eXchanger record information distributed through the DNS. A number of documents then specify how to convert or encode addresses between RFC822 style and the other mail system syntax. Those conversion methods give a smooth translation through an algorithm or a set of mapping rules, producing addresses indistinguishable from the native ones in both worlds.

MIXER describes a set of mappings, the MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping, that enable interworking between systems using the CCITT X.400 recommendations and systems using the RFC822 mail protocol. That work covers services, addresses, message envelopes and message bodies. This document concerns one aspect of it: the mechanism for mapping between X.400 originator and recipient addresses and RFC822 domain names. As described in Appendix F of MIXER, implementing the mappings requires a database that maps between X.400 addresses and domain names, and in the original design that database was statically defined.

The original approach required a lot of effort to maintain. All the gateways needed coherent tables so that they would apply the same mappings, the conversion tables had to be distributed among all the operational gateways, and every update had to be distributed too.

The concept of mapping rules distribution and use was revised in the newer MIXER specification, which introduced the idea of the MIXER Conformant Global Address Mapping. Such a mapping no longer has to be globally installed by every conformant gateway in the world, but MIXER does require efficient methods for publishing it. Static tables are one possible method, but they take a long time to modify and distribute, which puts heavy constraints on the schedule of every update. They also do not look feasible for distributing the database to the many other applications that need the rules, such as local address converters and mail user agents.

Two more efficient methods are proposed by MIXER for publishing the mapping: the Internet DNS and X.500. This memo is the complete technical specification for publishing it through the DNS. An earlier proposal by two of the authors of RFC 1664 used two new record types, TO-X400 and TO-822; this document adopts a more complete strategy and needs only one new record type. A first experiment used existing PTR records in a new tree under the .it top level domain, and the result was positive, with a few test applications running under that provisional setup. The experiment also showed the way to migrate, because name servers wishing to publish this information have to be modified to support the new record type and, in a large Internet with many implementations, that takes time.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way was a shared spreadsheet of rules. Every gateway needed the same copy, and every change had to reach every gateway. This RFC puts the rules where the Internet already keeps distributed, changeable information: the DNS.

sections.title: Why the DNS Rather Than Static Tables
sections.content:
Gateway implementations need a database holding the address mapping information for X.400 and RFC822, and that information has to be published to all MIXER gateways. The DNS has proved to be a practical way of providing a distributed name service. The RFC lists the advantages of a DNS-based system over a table-based one for mapping between X.400 addresses and domain names.

It avoids every host that wants to implement MIXER gateways or tools having to fetch and store entire mapping tables. Modifications to the DNS-based mapping information can be made available more quickly than with a table-driven approach. It allows full authority delegation, in agreement with the Internet regionalization process. Table management is not necessarily required for DNS-based MIXER gateways. And the mappings in use by a remote gateway can be determined by querying the DNS, which the RFC calls remote debugging.

Many other tools, such as address converters and user agents, can also take advantage of the real-time availability of the tables, which makes the information much easier to maintain.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS was already a distributed, delegated, always-current database, so putting the mapping rules in it means each organisation updates its own copy and everyone else picks the change up on the next lookup.

sections.title: The X.400 Name Space Inside the DNS
sections.content:
Domain names and their associated information, such as host addresses and mail exchanger names, are stored in the DNS as a distributed database under a number of top-level domains. Some top-level domains cover traditional categories or international organisations, such as EDU, COM, NET, ORG, INT and MIL, while every country has its own two-letter ISO country code as a top-level domain, including US for the United States. The special top-level and second-level couple IN-ADDR.ARPA stores the relationship between IP addresses and domain names. This memo defines the appropriate way to locate the X.400 address name space within that structure, so that the MIXER mappings can be stored in the DNS.

The mapping information is made of four tables. The 'table1' and 'gate1' tables give the translation from X.400 to RFC822, and the 'table2' and 'gate2' tables map RFC822 into X.400. Each table is made of mapping rules, and a single rule is made of a keyword, which is the argument of the mapping function derived from the address to be translated, and a translator, which is the parameter of the mapping function. The two are written as keyword#translator#, with the number sign delimiting the translator. An example is foo.bar.us#PRMD$foo\.bar.ADMD$intx.C$us#. Local mappings are not intended for use outside their restricted environment, so they should not be included in the DNS; if they are used they should be kept in static local tables, exactly as local static host tables can be used with DNS.

The keyword of a 'table2' or 'gate2' entry is a valid RFC822 domain, so the ordinary domain name space can hold those entries without trouble. The keyword of a 'table1' or 'gate1' entry, however, belongs to the X.400 address name space, which does not usually fit into the ordinary domain name space even though there are similarities, so a new name structure is needed. That structure has to be hooked to the existing domain name space in a way that respects the existing name hierarchy.

Creating another special branch from the root of the DNS tree, similar to the in-addr.arpa tree, would have required a central authority to coordinate at international level the management of each national X.400 name tree, including the public service providers. That is a heavy burden if approached globally, and the X.400 structure is very country oriented: it needs coordination at national level but has no concept of an international root, because the international X.400 service is based on a large number of bilateral agreements.

The two-letter ISO country codes used by X.400 are the same as those used for RFC822 country top-level domains, and that gives an immediate hook for the new branches. The proposal is to create under each national country code a new branch that represents exactly the X.400 name structure of that country, following the ADMD, PRMD, O and OU hierarchy. A unique reserved label, X42D, is placed under each country top-level domain, so that the national X.400 name space derives its own structure below it. For example, below the .it top-level domain sits X42D, and below that come labels such as ADMD-garr and ADMD-Master400, and below those labels for the private management domains such as PRMD-infn and PRMD-STET.

Putting the new tree at national level solves the international coordination problem, because the coordination simply moves to the national level and becomes easier to solve. The coordination between the X.400 communities and the Internet world is already required to create national static mapping tables, and using the DNS adds further motivation for it. It also lets each country set up its own X.400 structure and its own delegation on its own schedule, with no loss of global service in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules that translate a domain name into an X.400 address sit in the normal DNS tree, because a domain name is already a valid DNS name. The other direction needs a new home, and it gets one: a reserved label called X42D under each country code, so that the X.400 hierarchy becomes part of the DNS hierarchy.

sections.title: The PX Resource Record
sections.content:
The DNS specification in RFC 1035 provides resource records that hold specific pieces of information, including the Mail eXchanger record and the host address records used by Internet SMTP mailers. Because the mapping information is stored in the existing DNS tree, a new record type is needed to avoid any clash or misuse of existing data structures. The same new record is used for both directions of the mapping. It also gives room for the specific format and syntax of the mapping information, and leaves flexibility for future development.

The new record is called PX, standing for pointer to X.400 and RFC822 mapping information, in class IN, with value 26. Its RDATA holds three parts. PREFERENCE is a 16-bit integer giving the preference given to this record among others at the same owner name, where lower values are preferred. MAP822 is a domain-name element holding the RFC822 part of the mapping. MAPX400 is a domain-name element holding the value of the X.400 part of the mapping, written in the DNS syntax described below.

PX records cause no additional section processing and use the usual record format of name, optional class, optional time to live, type and RDATA. When a 'table1' or 'gate1' entry is stored, the name is an X.400 mail domain name in DNS syntax. When a 'table2' or 'gate2' entry is stored, the name is an RFC822 mail domain name, including both fully qualified DNS domains and mail-only domains used by MX records. All the normal DNS conventions apply to every component, and the name, MAP822 and MAPX400 must end with the root label when they are fully qualified.

The RFC then adds two features that the static MIXER tables do not have. The first is that DNS distinguishes an exact value from a wildcard match. Any MIXER entry is an implicit wildcard, so a rule covers any RFC822 domain ending with the given name unless more detailed rules exist for a subdomain, and there was no way to state an exact match only rule. In DNS, an entry beginning with the wildcard label gives the usual wildcard match, while an ordinary entry is valid only for an exact match of that domain. The second is the PREFERENCE value, which has the same meaning as the similar one in the MX record, so more than one mapping can be given for a domain with a preference order. Since the static tables cannot express either extension, the RFC strongly discourages using them when interoperating with a table-based gateway, and says the PREFERENCE value should be fixed at 50 and only wildcard names used for now.
sections.plainLanguage: One new DNS record type carries every mapping rule. It holds a preference number and the two addresses, and its name says which way the rule points.

sections.title: Writing an X.400 Address as a Domain Name
sections.content:
The MIXER syntax for mapping rules contains characters that have a special meaning in other DNS fields, so the RFC defines a syntax for the X.400 part of a rule that fits inside a domain-name element. A domain name is a series of labels separated by dots, and a label is made of letters, digits and interior hyphens. The legal character set for a label does not match the IA5 printable string set that MIXER uses, but a simple escape mechanism solves the problem.

The X.400 part of a mapping rule is written as a series of attributes separated by dots, where each attribute is a label, a dollar sign and a value. The attribute labels are C, ADMD, PRMD, O and OU, and the value may be a blank, an at sign or an IA5 printable string.

The translation rules are then simple. An attribute whose value is missing is written as the bare label. An attribute whose value is blank is written as the label followed by b. Anywhere else the label and the value are joined by a hyphen. Within the value, a hyphen becomes -h-, a quoted dot becomes -d-, a blank becomes -b-, and any character that is not a letter or a digit becomes its three-digit decimal code enclosed in hyphens. If the translation of the value ends with a hyphen, that last hyphen is dropped. A worked example turns OU$uuu.O$@.PRMD$ppp\.rrr.ADMD$aaa ddd-mmm.C$cc into OU-uuu.O.PRMD-ppp-d-rrr.ADMD-aaa-b-ddd-h-mmm.C-cc, and another turns OU$sales dept\..O$@.PRMD$ACME.ADMD$ .C$GB into OU-sales-b-dept-d.O.PRMD-ACME.ADMDb.C-GB. The RFC also gives a flow chart for each direction of the conversion, built on the rule that a string must be parsed from left to right, moving the pointer so that the already translated part is not looked at again.

There is one more convention. The X.400 country codes are the same as the RFC822 country top-level domains, so the C-cc part of an X.400 domain in domain-name syntax is omitted when the record name is created, because it is identical to the top-level country code identifying the zone where the information is stored. So ADMD$acme.C$fr becomes the key ADMD-acme.X42D.fr., and PRMD$ux\.av.ADMD$ .C$gb becomes PRMD-ux-d-av.ADMDb.X42D.gb..
sections.plainLanguage: An X.400 address uses characters that a DNS name cannot hold, so each awkward character is rewritten in a form the DNS accepts: a dot becomes -d-, a space becomes -b-, and anything else becomes its three-digit code.

sections.title: Finding the Mapping in the DNS
sections.content:
The mapping information is stored in the DNS both in the ordinary RFC822 domain name space and in the new X.400 name space. The information in a PX record does not represent a full RFC822 or X.400 address; it is a template that specifies the fields of the domain used by the mapping algorithm.

When the mapping information is in the DNS, queries are issued whenever an iterative search through the mapping table would have been performed. Because of the DNS search mechanism, DNS returns the longest possible match in the stored mapping rule with a single query, so no iteration or multiple queries are needed. A search of the mapping table results in either success, where the mapping is found, or failure, where the query fails and the mapping is not found.

A third possible result is a timeout. On a timeout the gateway operation is delayed and retried later. A success or a failure is processed according to the algorithms specified in MIXER. If a DNS error code is returned, an error message should be logged and the operation delayed as for a timeout. The RFC notes that these pathological situations should be avoided with careful duplication and caching, which DNS itself provides. Finding the name server that can authoritatively answer the query is done automatically by the DNS distributed name service.

The RFC works through examples. A gateway translating the address SUN.CCE.NRC.IT queries the DNS for the associated PX record, and the DNS may hold *.cce.nrc.it. IN PX 50 cce.nrc.it. O-cce.PRMD-nrc.ADMD-acme.C-it.. The first query returns the mapping rule in DNS storage format immediately. There is no .G. at the end of the RDATA, so applying the syntax translation gives a MIXER table 2 mapping rule.

If the gateway is looking for an RFC822 domain ending in the top-level domain MW and the DNS holds *.mw. IN PX 50 mw. O-cce.PRMD-nrc.ADMD-acme.C-it.G., the answer is a gate2 table entry in DNS storage format. Dropping the final .G. and applying the syntax translation gives the original rule, and the .G. flag also tells the gateway to use Domain Defined Attributes encoding for the domain it was asked about.

The other direction works the same way. Translating the address C=de; ADMD=pkz; PRMD=nfc; O=top; means converting the syntax, applying the country code convention to get the DNS name O-top.PRMD-nfc.ADMD-pkz.X42D.de., and querying for that. The DNS may hold *.ADMD-pkz.X42D.de. IN PX 50 pkz.de. ADMD-pkz.C-de., and the wildcard mechanism returns the table 1 rule in encoded form. A gate1 rule looks the same, with a .G. suffix in the RDATA, and the flag tells the gateway to use Left Hand Side encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: One DNS query finds the rule. The DNS returns the most specific match, so the gateway does not have to walk through a table of possibilities. A suffix on the answer tells the gateway whether it is looking at a direct mapping or at a gateway that should handle the address instead.

sections.title: Who Publishes the Mapping Information
sections.content:
The DNS with the PX record can distribute the mapping rules to all MIXER gateways on the Internet, but not every gateway will be able to use it. Some gateways in a management domain are expected to conform to a table-based, a DNS-based or an X.500-based model.

Table-based management domains will continue to publish their rules and retrieve the mapping tables through the International Mapping Table coordinator, manually or by some automated procedure. Their information can also be made available in DNS by the appropriate DNS authorities, using the same mechanism already in place for MX records: if a branch has not yet set up its own DNS server, a higher authority in the tree provides the service for it. A transition procedure similar to the one used to move from the hosts.txt tables to DNS can be applied to the deployment of this specification.

Coordination between the DNS and X.500 is more complex, because it requires uploading information between the two systems, though work on a dynamic alignment mechanism is already going on. The RFC reminds the reader that MIXER differs from the older approach of globally distributed, coordinated and unique mapping rules. MIXER no longer requires any conformant gateway or tool to know the complete set of mapping rules; it only requires that they use some set of valid rules, published by tables, DNS or X.500 or any combination, and it specifies that even incomplete sets may be used, with supplementary local unpublished rules to make up the difference. The coordination between the three publication systems is therefore not essential and matters only for operational efficiency.

One further point belongs with the operation of the records themselves. The 'gate1' and 'gate2' tables exist because an address cannot always be converted completely, so the address itself is encoded and points to the appropriate conformant gateway. The authority maintaining a DNS entry in the ordinary RFC822 space is the only one allowed to decide whether its domain is mapped using Standard Attributes or Domain Defined Attributes, and the authority maintaining an entry in the new X.400 space is the only one allowed to decide between Standard Attributes and Left Hand Side encoding. There can therefore be no two possible entries for one domain, and the action for a gateway is clearly stated. A gateway or other application can tell which kind of information it got because the RDATA carries an additional .G. post-fix when it holds a gate entry, which creates no conflict because every X.400 domain ends with a country code. That post-fix must be removed before the data is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Organisations publish their own rules simply by being given the DNS delegation for their part of the tree. The DNS decides who is allowed to publish, and the owner of a branch decides whether its addresses are mapped directly or sent to a gateway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document notes that PX records direct the translation between X.400 addresses and Internet mail addresses, and that this can indirectly affect the routing of mail across a gateway. A successful attack on the service could cause an incorrect translation of an originator address, which amounts to forging that address, or an incorrect translation of a recipient address, which could direct mail to an unauthorized recipient or make it appear to an authorized recipient that the message was intended for other recipients. It could also force the mail path through a particular gateway or message transfer agent where mail security can be affected by compromised software.

Several means by which an attacker might deliver incorrect PX records to a client are listed: compromise of a DNS server, generating a counterfeit response to a client's DNS query, and returning incorrect additional information in response to an unrelated query.

Clients using PX records should therefore ensure that routing and address translations are based only on authoritative answers. Once DNS security mechanisms become more widely deployed, clients should employ those mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of PX records.
sections.plainLanguage: A wrong answer from the DNS can put mail in the wrong place or make it look as though it came from someone else. The advice is to trust only authoritative answers, and to use DNS security once it is widely available.

items.title: Three publication methods
items.text: A management domain may publish its mapping with static tables, with DNS, with X.500, or with any combination.

items.title: Partial rules are allowed
items.text: A gateway only needs some valid rules, and incomplete sets may be used, with local unpublished rules to fill the gaps.

items.title: Delegation follows the DNS
items.text: An organisation publishes its mapping simply by being given delegation for its branch of the X.400 name space.

items.title: A gradual rollout
items.text: The first deployment is centralised, and authority is delegated step by step, in the way the DNS itself grew.
